---
title: "Experimental design"
---

Suppose we want to compare how listeners recognize words in two accents. Before collecting responses, we must decide which participants and words may enter the study, which unit receives an accent condition, which responses are measured, and which observations are retained for analysis. These decisions determine the comparison that will be available after collection.

Recall that the [unit represented by one row](../foundations/linguistic-data.qmd) need not be the unit that receives a condition. If accent is assigned once per participant, then all trials from that participant receive the same assignment. A dataset with 2,000 trial rows from 40 participants still contains 40 independently assigned units, not 2,000.

The design must also permit estimation of the [intended contrast](../foundations/making-sense-of-data.qmd). If the target is a mean difference between two training procedures, the design must produce comparable groups that differ in training procedure. A regression model fitted after collection cannot distinguish training from a preexisting group difference if the design confounded them.

::: {.callout-note title="Reading: Winter (2020), Sections 14.2 and 14.3"}
[Winter, *The independence assumption* and *Dealing with non-independence via experimental design and averaging*, in *Statistics for Linguists*](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf).

**Why this reading?** These sections begin with the repeated observations common in linguistic research and ask which observations may count as independent evidence. They are included here because the same question governs assignment, counterbalancing, exclusion, and design simulation throughout this module.
:::

## Assignment and comparison

The [unit of assignment](units-of-assignment.qmd) is the entity that can independently receive a condition. The [random assignment mechanism](random-assignment.qmd) is the probability rule used to allocate conditions to those units.

In a [within-participant design](within-participant-designs.qmd), each participant contributes responses in more than one condition. The comparison can thus be made within participants, though order and carryover may matter. In a [between-participant design](between-participant-designs.qmd), each participant contributes to only one condition, so the condition difference is also a difference between participant groups.

[Counterbalancing](counterbalancing.qmd) distributes item versions across experimental lists. A participant should not see several versions of the same item, but each item must occur in each condition across the complete design if the intended contrast is within items.

## Retention and power

[Exclusion rules](exclusion-rules.qmd) determine which assigned observations enter the analysis. If nonresponses occur more often in one accent and are removed, the retained comparison concerns trials on which a response was produced. The exclusion rule is thus part of the estimand.

[Power by simulation](power-by-simulation.qmd) evaluates the planned assignment, data-generating process, exclusion rule, model, and decision procedure together. Varying plausible effect sizes and sources of variation shows how often the complete procedure reaches its stated decision under those assumptions.
